title: Roth IRA and Social Security (Does a Roth Affect SS?)
subtitle: Roth IRA withdrawals do not count as provisional income for Social Security taxation. Traditional IRA withdrawals do. Up to 85% of SS can be taxable — Roth keeps that ceiling lower.
source_irs: IRS Pub 915; SSA Publication No. 05-10069; IRC §86 (Social Security taxation)

concepts.heading: The Rule
concepts.lede: Roth IRA withdrawals are not part of the Social Security provisional income formula. Traditional IRA withdrawals are.
body: Provisional income = other income + 50% of SS benefits + tax-exempt interest.
If provisional income > $34,000 single / $44,000 MFJ, up to 50% of SS becomes taxable.
If provisional income > $44,000 single / $64,000 MFJ, up to 85% of SS becomes taxable.
Roth withdrawals don't enter this formula. Trad IRA withdrawals do.

concepts.heading: The Tax Gap
concepts.lede: Same $50,000 withdrawal — from a Trad IRA, you owe tax on the SS bump. From a Roth, you don't.
body: Scenario: you're 67, on SS, taking $50K/yr for living expenses.
Trad IRA: $50K adds to provisional income. Up to $42,500 of your SS becomes taxable. Effective tax: $10,000+ on the SS portion alone.
Roth IRA: $50K doesn't count. Your SS stays as low-taxed as possible. No SS taxation bump.

concepts.heading: The Strategy
concepts.lede: Build the Roth so you can manage your provisional income in retirement. Trad IRAs force you into higher tax brackets when SS kicks in.
body: Goal: provisional income under $34K single / $44K MFJ in early retirement years.
Use Roth for the dollars you can convert/withdraw without bumping SS taxation.
Trad IRA dollars: defer to age 70+ when RMDs force them out anyway.
